claim: Measurably evolving populations are systems that undergo evolution rapidly enough for significant genetic differences to be detected in longitudinally sampled timepoints.
source: Measurably evolving populations are systems that undergo evolution rapidly enough for significant genetic differences to be detected in longitudinally sampled timepoints (Drummond et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Drummond et al., 2003, which establishes this as a concept from prior literature.

claim: B cells experience similarly rapid evolution during affinity maturation as viruses such as HIV and SARS-CoV-2.
source: While this concept is frequently applied to viruses such as HIV (Rambaut et al., 2004) and SARS-CoV-2 (e.g., du Plessis et al., 2021), B cells experience similarly rapid evolution during affinity maturation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on viral evolution (Rambaut et al., 2004; du Plessis et al., 2021) and draws on established knowledge about B cell affinity maturation.

claim: B cell affinity maturation is critical for developing high-affinity antibodies in response to infection and vaccination.
source: B cell affinity maturation is critical for developing high-affinity antibodies in response to infection and vaccination (Shlomchik and Weisel, 2012; Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shlomchik and Weisel, 2012 and Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012.

claim: Somatic hypermutation introduces mutations into the B cell receptor loci at a rate orders of magnitude higher than the background rate of somatic mutations.
source: During affinity maturation, somatic hypermutation (SHM) introduces mutations into the B cell receptor (BCR) loci at a rate orders of magnitude higher than the background rate of somatic mutations (McKean et al., 1984; Murphy et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McKean et al., 1984 and Murphy et al., 2008.

claim: Modified BCRs are selected based on their binding affinity during affinity maturation.
source: These modified BCRs are selected based on their binding affinity, and the process repeats cyclically within germinal centers (GCs Teng and Papavasiliou, 2007; Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Teng and Papavasiliou, 2007 and Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012.

claim: Infection or vaccination can stimulate pre-existing memory B cells that rapidly differentiate into antibody secreting plasmablasts or possibly re-enter GCs to undergo additional affinity maturation.
source: Infection or vaccination can also stimulate pre-existing memory B cells that rapidly differentiate into antibody secreting plasmablasts or possibly re-enter GCs to undergo additional affinity maturation (Ellebedy, 2018; Mesin et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ellebedy, 2018 and Mesin et al., 2020.

claim: A lack of vaccine-specific affinity maturation is thought to underlie the poor efficacy of seasonal influenza virus vaccination.
source: A lack of vaccine-specific affinity maturation is thought to underlie the poor efficacy of seasonal influenza virus vaccination (Arevalo et al., 2020; Ellebedy, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arevalo et al., 2020 and Ellebedy, 2018.

claim: Antigen-specific B cell lineages can be recruited into GCs following influenza vaccination.
source: While recent work has shown that antigen-specific B cell lineages can be recruited into GCs following influenza vaccination (Turner et al., 2020), other work has been unable to detect significant increases in SHM frequency among circulating influenza-binding antibody lineages following vaccination (Ellebedy et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Turner et al., 2020.

claim: Other work has been unable to detect significant increases in SHM frequency among circulating influenza-binding antibody lineages following vaccination.
source: While recent work has shown that antigen-specific B cell lineages can be recruited into GCs following influenza vaccination (Turner et al., 2020), other work has been unable to detect significant increases in SHM frequency among circulating influenza-binding antibody lineages following vaccination (Ellebedy et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ellebedy et al., 2016.

claim: The date randomization test detected measurable evolution in 47% of lineages after 10 additional GC cycles in simulations.
source: Using this framework in which all lineages are evolving, the date randomization test detected measurable evolution in 47% of lineages after 10 additional GC cycles, and 77% after 15 additional cycles (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: The date randomization test detected measurable evolution in 77% of lineages after 15 additional GC cycles in simulations.
source: Using this framework in which all lineages are evolving, the date randomization test detected measurable evolution in 47% of lineages after 10 additional GC cycles, and 77% after 15 additional cycles (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: A GC cycle time of 6–24 hr means 15 cycles corresponds to 4–15 days.
source: Given a GC cycle time of 6–24 hr, 15 cycles corresponds to 4–15 days, within the timeframe of many longitudinal B cell repertoire studies (Ellebedy et al., 2016; Laserson et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on a mathematical calculation from known GC cycle times and is supported by citations to studies with relevant timeframes.

claim: The date randomization test had higher power to detect measurable evolution in simulations of neutral evolution than those that included selection.
source: Interestingly, the date randomization test had higher power to detect measurable evolution in simulations of neutral evolution than those that included selection (Figure 1—figure supplements 3–4).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1—figure supplements 3–4.

claim: Selection can reduce the rate of divergence within lineages compared to neutral evolution.
source: This is likely because selection can reduce the rate of divergence within lineages compared to neutral evolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The date randomization test found measurable evolution in <4% of simulations with randomized sample time associations.
source: To quantify the false positive rate, we repeated these calculations on the same simulations but with randomized sample time associations. Here, the date randomization test found measurable evolution in <4% in each case, indicating a low false positive rate (Figure 1—figure supplements 3–4).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1—figure supplements 3–4.

claim: Primary immune responses are enriched for measurably evolving lineages.
source: Confirming our hypothesis, we observed an enrichment of measurably evolving lineages (>5% of tested lineages) in primary immune responses including HIV infection, meningococcus vaccination, primary but not secondary hepatitis B vaccination, and early childhood development (Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HIV infection is enriched for measurably evolving lineages.
source: Confirming our hypothesis, we observed an enrichment of measurably evolving lineages (>5% of tested lineages) in primary immune responses including HIV infection, meningococcus vaccination, primary but not secondary hepatitis B vaccination, and early childhood development (Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Meningococcus vaccination is enriched for measurably evolving lineages.
source: Confirming our hypothesis, we observed an enrichment of measurably evolving lineages (>5% of tested lineages) in primary immune responses including HIV infection, meningococcus vaccination, primary but not secondary hepatitis B vaccination, and early childhood development (Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Primary hepatitis B vaccination is enriched for measurably evolving lineages.
source: Confirming our hypothesis, we observed an enrichment of measurably evolving lineages (>5% of tested lineages) in primary immune responses including HIV infection, meningococcus vaccination, primary but not secondary hepatitis B vaccination, and early childhood development (Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Secondary hepatitis B vaccination is not enriched for measurably evolving lineages.
source: Confirming our hypothesis, we observed an enrichment of measurably evolving lineages (>5% of tested lineages) in primary immune responses including HIV infection, meningococcus vaccination, primary but not secondary hepatitis B vaccination, and early childhood development (Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Early childhood development is enriched for measurably evolving lineages.
source: Confirming our hypothesis, we observed an enrichment of measurably evolving lineages (>5% of tested lineages) in primary immune responses including HIV infection, meningococcus vaccination, primary but not secondary hepatitis B vaccination, and early childhood development (Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HIV infection was more enriched for measurably evolving lineages than other conditions surveyed, with each study having between 5.9% and 53% of lineages measurably evolving.
source: Consistent with this arms race, HIV infection was more enriched for measurably evolving lineages than other conditions surveyed, with each study having between 5.9% and 53% of lineages measurably evolving (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Lineages from subjects with broadly neutralizing anti-HIV lineages sampled over multiple years were particularly enriched (26–53% measurably evolving).
source: Lineages from subjects with broadly neutralizing anti-HIV lineages sampled over multiple years (Doria-Rose et al., 2014; Landais et al., 2017; Liao et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2015) were particularly enriched (26–53% measurably evolving).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from multiple cited studies (Doria-Rose et al., 2014; Landais et al., 2017; Liao et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2015).

claim: HIV studies included were sampled over longer time periods than studies of other conditions (mean = 225 vs 45 weeks).
source: Importantly, the HIV studies included were sampled over longer time periods than studies of other conditions (mean = 225 vs 45 weeks, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Truncated HIV datasets (first 60 weeks) were still highly enriched for measurably evolving lineages (6.9–64%) compared to other non-HIV datasets with similar sampling intervals (0–7.2%).
source: These truncated datasets were still highly enriched for measurably evolving lineages (6.9–64%) compared to other non-HIV datasets with similar sampling intervals (0–7.2%, Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: B cell lineages from healthy children sampled during the first 3 years of life were enriched for measurable evolution (14%).
source: B cell lineages from healthy children sampled during the first 3 years of life were enriched for measurable evolution (14%), possibly reflecting continual exposure to novel antigens (Nielsen et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Nielsen et al., 2019.

claim: An enrichment of measurably evolving lineages was observed following primary meningococcus vaccination (10%).
source: We also observed an enrichment of measurably evolving lineages following primary meningococcus vaccination (10%; Galson et al., 2015a) and primary but not secondary hepatitis B vaccination (7.2% vs 2.9%, respectively; Galson et al., 2016; Galson et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Galson et al., 2015a.

claim: An enrichment of measurably evolving lineages was observed following primary hepatitis B vaccination (7.2%) but not secondary hepatitis B vaccination (2.9%).
source: We also observed an enrichment of measurably evolving lineages following primary meningococcus vaccination (10%; Galson et al., 2015a) and primary but not secondary hepatitis B vaccination (7.2% vs 2.9%, respectively; Galson et al., 2016; Galson et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Galson et al., 2016 and Galson et al., 2015b.

claim: Allergen-specific immunotherapy was enriched for measurable evolution (6.5%).
source: Further, allergen-specific immunotherapy, which stimulates tolerance of allergy-causing antigens through exposure, was also enriched for measurable evolution (6.5%; Levin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Levin et al., 2016.

claim: Ebola virus infection showed a borderline (5%) percentage of measurably evolving lineages.
source: Interestingly, Ebola virus infection showed a borderline (5%) percentage of measurably evolving lineages (Table 1) despite likely being a primary infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Measurably evolving lineages were more likely to contain mAbs than nonmeasurably evolving lineages (p = 0.031).
source: We found that across these studies measurably evolving lineages were more likely to contain mAbs than nonmeasurably evolving lineages (p = 0.031, Wilcoxon test, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon test) of data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Between 2.9% and 5.2% of lineages were measurably evolving across three adult influenza vaccine datasets.
source: Across subjects in each study, between only 2.9% and 5.2% of lineages were measurably evolving (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: The 4- to 13-week sampling range of influenza studies was sufficiently long to detect ongoing affinity maturation with high sensitivity (>90%).
source: To verify the 4- to 13-week sampling range of these studies was sufficient to detect measurable evolution, we performed simulation analyses replicating the sampling strategy of the influenza dataset with the shortest sampling range (Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Laserson et al., 2014). These simulations show this timescale was sufficiently long to detect ongoing affinity maturation with high sensitivity (>90%, Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Figure 1H.

claim: 15 lineages in influenza datasets had adjusted date randomization p values < 0.1.
source: We identified 15 lineages in influenza datasets, and 354 lineages in other conditions, with adjusted date randomization p values < 0.1.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.

claim: 354 lineages in other conditions had adjusted date randomization p values < 0.1.
source: We identified 15 lineages in influenza datasets, and 354 lineages in other conditions, with adjusted date randomization p values < 0.1.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.

claim: Lineages from influenza vaccination had significantly higher initial divergence (median = 8.6%) than those from early HIV infection (median = 5%, p = 0.0012).
source: Consistent with memory B cell reactivation, lineages from influenza vaccination had significantly higher initial divergence (median = 8.6%) than those from primary responses such as early HIV infection (median = 5%, p = 0.0012) and primary hepatitis B vaccination (median = 2.8%, p = 0.0019) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Lineages from influenza vaccination had significantly higher initial divergence (median = 8.6%) than those from primary hepatitis B vaccination (median = 2.8%, p = 0.0019).
source: Consistent with memory B cell reactivation, lineages from influenza vaccination had significantly higher initial divergence (median = 8.6%) than those from primary responses such as early HIV infection (median = 5%, p = 0.0012) and primary hepatitis B vaccination (median = 2.8%, p = 0.0019) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Measurably evolving lineages showed evidence of purifying selection (mean ωCDR = 0.58, mean ωFWR = 0.48).
source: Across all conditions surveyed, we found evidence of purifying selection operating on adjusted measurably evolving lineages (mean ωCDR = 0.58, mean ωFWR = 0.48, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 2.

claim: ωCDR was significantly <1 in 10/13 subjects.
source: We found that ωCDR was significantly <1 in 10/13 subjects (significantly >1 in none) and ωFWR was significantly <1 in 13/13 subjects (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (phylogenetic likelihood ratio test) of data presented in Table 2.

claim: ωFWR was significantly <1 in 13/13 subjects.
source: We found that ωCDR was significantly <1 in 10/13 subjects (significantly >1 in none) and ωFWR was significantly <1 in 13/13 subjects (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (phylogenetic likelihood ratio test) of data presented in Table 2.

claim: 7.5% of lineages containing sequences from GC B cells were measurably evolving, compared to only 3.0% of lineages with no identified GC sequences.
source: We found that 7.5% of lineages containing sequences from GC B cells were measurably evolving, compared to only 3.0% of lineages with no identified GC sequences.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of GC-associated lineages.

claim: 10% of lineages containing ≥10% GC sequences were measurably evolving.
source: For instance, while 10% of lineages containing ≥10% GC sequences were measurably evolving, 38% (3/8) of those with ≥25% GC sequences were measurably evolving (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: 38% (3/8) of lineages with ≥25% GC sequences were measurably evolving.
source: For instance, while 10% of lineages containing ≥10% GC sequences were measurably evolving, 38% (3/8) of those with ≥25% GC sequences were measurably evolving (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Lineages with higher proportions of GC sequences had a higher correlation between divergence and time (linear regression slope = 1.1, p = 8.9 × 10−13).
source: Lineages with higher proportions of GC sequences also had a higher correlation between divergence and time (linear regression slope = 1.1, p = 8.9 × 10−13, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (linear regression) of data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In all 10,000 bootstrap resampling repetitions, the slope of the linear regression between GC sequence proportion and the correlation between divergence and time was positive.
source: We found that in all 10,000 resampling repetitions, the slope of the linear regression between GC sequence proportion and the correlation between divergence and time was positive, with 95% of repetitions having a slope between 0.81 and 1.3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by bootstrap analysis presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Measurably evolving lineages with the highest proportion of GC sequences contained mAbs that bound to vaccine antigens.
source: Finally, the measurably evolving lineages with the highest proportion of GC sequences contained mAbs that bound to vaccine antigens (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Measurably evolving lineages with the highest proportion of GC sequences show signs of origin from memory B cells, such as clonal relatedness to blood plasmablasts sampled 5 days postvaccination.
source: These lineages show signs of origin from memory B cells, such as clonal relatedness to blood plasmablasts sampled 5 days postvaccination, and high mean germline divergence at their first sampled timepoint (6.3%, 7.2%, Figure 3B, C, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Measurably evolving lineages with the highest proportion of GC sequences had high mean germline divergence at their first sampled timepoint (6.3%, 7.2%).
source: These lineages show signs of origin from memory B cells, such as clonal relatedness to blood plasmablasts sampled 5 days postvaccination, and high mean germline divergence at their first sampled timepoint (6.3%, 7.2%, Figure 3B, C, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Chronic HIV infection stimulates ongoing affinity maturation as B cells evolve to contain viral escape mutants.
source: Chronic HIV infection stimulates ongoing affinity maturation as B cells evolve to contain viral escape mutants (Liao et al., 2013; Wendel et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liao et al., 2013 and Wendel et al., 2020.

claim: A substantial fraction of longitudinally sampled B cell lineages within the repertoires of subjects with HIV are measurably evolving.
source: This signature is not limited to single lineages. Rather, a substantial fraction of longitudinally sampled B cell lineages within the repertoires of subjects with HIV are measurably evolving, consistent with clonal competition among B cell lineages during HIV infection (Nourmohammad et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and a citation to Nourmohammad et al., 2019.

claim: Early childhood development during the first 3 years of life showed the second-highest enrichment of measurably evolving lineages among surveyed conditions.
source: Early childhood development during the first 3 years of life (Nielsen et al., 2019) showed the second-highest enrichment of measurably evolving lineages among surveyed conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and a citation to Nielsen et al., 2019.

claim: Primary vaccinations (meningococcus, primary hepatitis B) showed stronger signatures of measurable evolution than secondary vaccinations (adult seasonal influenza, hepatitis B booster).
source: Further, primary vaccinations (meningococcus, primary hepatitis B)(Galson et al., 2016; Galson et al., 2015a) showed stronger signatures of measurable evolution than secondary vaccinations (adult seasonal influenza, hepatitis B booster) (Ellebedy et al., 2016; Galson et al., 2015b; Laserson et al., 2014; Turner et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and citations to multiple studies.

claim: A strong signal of purifying selection is a straightforward prediction of evolution toward an adaptive peak.
source: Though perhaps counterintuitive, a strong signal of purifying selection is a straightforward prediction of evolution toward an adaptive peak (Hoehn et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hoehn et al., 2019.

claim: Similar evidence of purifying selection during affinity maturation has been observed in other studies including influenza vaccination, HIV infection, and healthy controls.
source: Similar evidence of purifying selection during affinity maturation has been observed in other studies including influenza vaccination, HIV infection, and healthy controls (Cizmeci et al., 2021; Hoehn et al., 2019; Sheng et al., 2016; Yaari et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cizmeci et al., 2021; Hoehn et al., 2019; Sheng et al., 2016; and Yaari et al., 2015.

claim: Seasonal influenza virus vaccination in young adults induces a GC reaction where maturation of vaccine-specific B cell lineages occurs, including those likely recruited from the pre-existing memory B cell compartment.
source: We find that seasonal influenza virus vaccination in young adults induces a GC reaction where maturation of vaccine-specific B cell lineages occurs, including those likely recruited from the pre-existing memory B cell compartment.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Poor efficacy of seasonal influenza vaccination does not result from a complete lack of vaccine-induced B cell evolution.
source: These results imply that poor efficacy of seasonal influenza vaccination does not result from a complete lack of vaccine-induced B cell evolution.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SHM occurs at ~10−3 SHM/bp/division in mice.
source: Studies in mice have estimated that SHM occurs at ~10−3 SHM/bp/division (Kleinstein et al., 2003; McKean et al., 1984), and that GC B cells cycle every 6–12 hr (Allen et al., 2007; Hauser et al., 2007; Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kleinstein et al., 2003 and McKean et al., 1984.

claim: GC B cells cycle every 6–12 hr in mice.
source: Studies in mice have estimated that SHM occurs at ~10−3 SHM/bp/division (Kleinstein et al., 2003; McKean et al., 1984), and that GC B cells cycle every 6–12 hr (Allen et al., 2007; Hauser et al., 2007; Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Allen et al., 2007; Hauser et al., 2007; and Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012.

claim: The date randomization test is implemented within the Immcantation.org framework in the R package dowser.
source: This test is implemented within the Immcantation.org framework in the R package dowser (Hoehn et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hoehn et al., 2020.

claim: Influenza vaccination stimulates memory B cell lineages with high SHM frequency.
source: While influenza vaccination stimulates memory B cell lineages with high SHM frequency (Laserson et al., 2014; Wrammert et al., 2008), these lineages are only measurably evolving if their level of SHM detectably increases during the sampling interval surrounding vaccination.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Laserson et al., 2014 and Wrammert et al., 2008.

claim: While most circulating lineages following influenza virus vaccination are not measurably evolving, a subset of memory B cell lineages re-enter GCs and increase in SHM frequency.
source: We further show that while most circulating lineages following influenza virus vaccination are not measurably evolving, a subset of memory B cell lineages re-enter GCs and increase in SHM frequency.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Clustering based on nucleotide sequence similarity detects clonal relationships with high confidence.
source: After preprocessing the sequencing data, we first identify clonal lineages – B cells that descend from a common V(D)J rearrangement – using clustering based on nucleotide sequence similarity, which we have previously shown detects clonal relationships with high confidence (Gupta et al., 2017; Zhou and Kleinstein, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gupta et al., 2017 and Zhou and Kleinstein, 2019.

claim: In evolving lineages, sequences sampled at later timepoints are expected to have higher divergence than those from earlier timepoints.
source: In evolving lineages, sequences sampled at later timepoints are expected to have higher divergence than those from earlier timepoints (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about evolution and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Datasets with >5% measurably evolving lineages are referred to as 'enriched' for measurable evolution.
source: We therefore refer to datasets with >5% measurably evolving lineages as 'enriched' for measurable evolution.
evidence: The claim is an explicit definition provided by the authors.

claim: 1/10 of influenza-binding lineages found only in the blood were measurably evolving.
source: While 1/10 of influenza-binding lineages found only in the blood were measurably evolving, 2/5 lineages with >25% GC sequences were measurably evolving (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: 2/5 influenza-binding lineages with >25% GC sequences were measurably evolving.
source: While 1/10 of influenza-binding lineages found only in the blood were measurably evolving, 2/5 lineages with >25% GC sequences were measurably evolving (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Many later-sampled GC sequences are more diverged than earlier-sampled sequences within the measurably evolving, influenza-binding lineages.
source: Instead, many later-sampled GC sequences are clearly more diverged than earlier-sampled sequences within the measurably evolving, influenza-binding lineages we observed (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The uniform permutation test had a high rate of negatively evolving lineages (mean = 8.3%), indicating a high false positive rate.
source: We found the uniform permutation test had a high rate of negatively evolving lineages (mean = 8.3%), indicating a high false positive rate.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The clustered permutation test without resolved polytomies had a mean rate of only 2.2% negatively evolving lineages.
source: By contrast, the clustered permutation test without resolved polytomies had a mean rate of only 2.2% negatively evolving lineages, approximately as expected given an alpha value of 0.025.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Resolving polytomies and then performing the clustered permutation test resulted in a mean rate of 1.2% negatively evolving lineages.
source: Resolving polytomies and then performing the clustered permutation test improved performance even more, with a mean rate of 1.2% negatively evolving lineages and no dataset having more than 2.8% of lineages negatively evolving.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.
